title: Information Theory
description: Entropy, cross-entropy, KL divergence and mutual information, and their role in loss functions, decision trees and generative models.
overview: Information theory, created by Claude Shannon in 1948, measures uncertainty and information in bits. It began as a theory of communication, asking how compactly a message can be encoded and how much can be sent through a noisy channel. It supplies the vocabulary of modern machine learning: the cross-entropy loss, the KL divergence in variational inference and reinforcement learning, the mutual information behind decision-tree splits, and the perplexity of a language model.
This chapter defines entropy, cross-entropy, KL divergence and mutual information, proves their basic properties, connects them to coding, and shows how each appears in the Machine Learning book.
objectives: Compute the entropy of a discrete distribution in bits and nats, and explain it as expected surprise and as the optimal code length.
Compute joint and conditional entropy and mutual information from a joint table.
Define cross-entropy and KL divergence, prove that KL ≥ 0, and compute them for small distributions.
Explain why maximum likelihood minimizes the KL divergence and why the cross-entropy is the classification loss.
Compute the entropy and KL divergence of Gaussians and describe forward and reverse KL.

sections.title: Entropy
body: How surprised are you when you learn that it rained today? If you live in a rainforest, hardly at all. If you live in a desert, a lot. The rarer an event, the more surprising, and the more information it carries. Now average that surprise over all the possible outcomes, weighted by how often each occurs: that average is the entropy, a measure of how unpredictable the source is. A fair coin is as unpredictable as a two-outcome source can be, and a coin that nearly always lands heads is quite predictable. The **information** (surprise) of an event with probability p is −log p: rare events are surprising and carry much information, and certain events carry none. With logarithms to base 2 the unit is the **bit**, and with natural logarithms the **nat** (1 nat = 1.443 bits). The **entropy** of a discrete random variable is its expected surprise:

body.eq: H(X) = −Σ_x p(x) log p(x) = E[ −log p(X) ]

body: with the convention 0 log 0 = 0. Entropy measures uncertainty: it is zero when the outcome is certain and largest when all outcomes are equally likely. For n equally likely outcomes, H = log n.

body.caption: The binary entropy H(p) = −p log₂ p − (1 − p) log₂(1 − p) is zero at p = 0 and 1 and reaches its maximum of 1 bit at p = 0.5.

example.title: Entropy of a coin
example.problem: Compute the entropy of a fair coin and of a coin with P(heads) = 0.1.
example.solution: Fair: −2(0.5 log₂ 0.5) = 1 bit. Biased: −0.1 log₂ 0.1 − 0.9 log₂ 0.9 = 0.1(3.322) + 0.9(0.152) = 0.332 + 0.137 = 0.469 bits. The biased coin is more predictable, so each flip carries less than half a bit of information.

body: Entropy is the answer to a practical question: how many bits per symbol are needed, on average, to encode a stream of independent symbols drawn from p? Shannon's source coding theorem says that the best possible average length L of a code for which no codeword is a prefix of another satisfies H(X) ≤ L < H(X) + 1 bits per symbol. A symbol with probability p should get a codeword of length about −log₂ p: frequent symbols get short codes. **Huffman coding** achieves the optimum.

example.title: A Huffman code
example.problem: Symbols A, B, C, D have probabilities 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/8. Find the entropy and a Huffman code.
example.solution: H = ½(1) + ¼(2) + ⅛(3) + ⅛(3) = 1.75 bits. A Huffman code is A = 0, B = 10, C = 110, D = 111, with lengths 1, 2, 3, 3 and average 0.5(1) + 0.25(2) + 0.125(3) + 0.125(3) = 1.75 bits. Because every probability is a power of 1/2, the code meets the entropy exactly, against 2 bits for a fixed-length code.

sections.title: Joint entropy, conditional entropy and mutual information
body: For two variables, the **joint entropy** is H(X, Y) = −ΣΣ p(x, y) log p(x, y), and the **conditional entropy** H(Y | X) = Σ_x p(x)H(Y | X = x) is the uncertainty remaining in Y once X is known. They satisfy the **chain rule**
and conditioning never increases entropy, H(Y | X) ≤ H(Y), with equality exactly when X and Y are independent. The reduction in uncertainty is the **mutual information**:

body.eq: I(X; Y) = H(Y) − H(Y | X) = Σ p(x, y) log [ p(x, y) / (p(x)p(y)) ]

body: It is symmetric, non-negative, and zero iff X and Y are independent. Unlike correlation, mutual information detects any kind of dependence, linear or not (for Y = X² with X symmetric, the correlation is zero but the mutual information is positive).

example.title: Mutual information from a joint table
example.problem: For the joint distribution P(0, 0) = 0.3, P(0, 1) = 0.2, P(1, 0) = 0.1, P(1, 1) = 0.4 (Multivariate Probability), compute I(X; Y) in bits.
solution: The marginals are P(X) = (0.5, 0.5) and P(Y) = (0.4, 0.6). Terms p log₂[p/(p_xp_y)]:
The sum is I(X; Y) = 0.125 bits. Knowing X removes about 0.125 of the 0.971 bits of uncertainty in Y: the dependence is real but weak.

list: **Decision trees**: the information gain of a split on feature X for label Y is exactly I(X; Y) = H(Y) − H(Y | X) (see Decision Trees).
**Feature selection** ranks features by their mutual information with the target.

**Data processing inequality**: if X → Y → Z is a Markov chain, I(X; Z) ≤ I(X; Y). No processing of Y, however clever, can create information about X. Each layer of a network can only lose information about the input; the art is to lose the irrelevant part.
**Representation learning**: contrastive methods maximize a lower bound on the mutual information between two views of the data.

sections.title: Cross-entropy and KL divergence
body: Suppose a language really uses the letter E 12% of the time but you design your shorthand assuming all 26 letters are equally likely. Your shorthand gives E a long code, so your messages come out longer than necessary. The extra length is the price of using the wrong model. Cross-entropy is the total average length with the wrong model, and the KL divergence is the extra part, the waste. If your assumed model is perfect, the waste is zero. How well does a model distribution q describe data that actually follow p? If we encode symbols drawn from p using a code designed for q, the average length is the **cross-entropy**

body.eq: H(p, q) = −Σ_x p(x) log q(x) = H(p) + KL(p ‖ q)

body: where the extra cost is the **Kullback–Leibler divergence** (relative entropy):

body.eq: KL(p ‖ q) = Σ_x p(x) log ( p(x) / q(x) ) = E_p [ log p(X) − log q(X) ]

body.key: Gibbs' inequality: KL(p ‖ q) ≥ 0, with equality iff p = q.

body: **Proof.** Use ln y ≤ y − 1 with y = q/p: −KL = Σ p ln(q/p) ≤ Σ p (q/p − 1) = Σq − Σp = 1 − 1 = 0. ∎ (Jensen's inequality gives the same.) Therefore no model can code p more cheaply than its entropy: H(p, q) ≥ H(p).

KL is **not symmetric** and not a metric (it violates the triangle inequality), though it is the standard way to measure how far a model is from the truth. The symmetrized Jensen–Shannon divergence appears in the GAN objective.

example.title: KL in both directions
example.problem: For p = (0.5, 0.5) and q = (0.9, 0.1), compute H(p), H(p, q), KL(p ‖ q) and KL(q ‖ p) in bits.

body: Minimizing KL(p ‖ q) over q (the **forward** KL, used in maximum likelihood) penalizes q heavily wherever p has mass but q has little: q must cover all of p, and is **mass-covering**. Minimizing the **reverse** KL(q ‖ p) (used in variational inference) penalizes q for putting mass where p has little, so q tends to lock onto a single mode of p and underestimate its spread: it is **mode-seeking**. Fitting a single Gaussian to a bimodal p gives a broad Gaussian covering both modes with the forward KL, and a narrow Gaussian on one mode with the reverse KL.

list: KL(p ‖ q) is infinite if q(x) = 0 for some x with p(x) > 0. This is why smoothing is needed and why language models never assign zero probability.
For continuous distributions replace sums by integrals; the KL divergence stays non-negative and invariant to invertible changes of variable.

sections.title: Information theory in machine learning
body: **Maximum likelihood is KL minimization.** Let p_data be the true distribution and p_θ the model. Then

The entropy of the data does not depend on θ, so minimizing the KL divergence is the same as maximizing E_{p_data}[log p_θ(x)], which the sample average Σ log p_θ(x_i)/m estimates. The cross-entropy loss −log p_θ(y | x) used to train classifiers is therefore the empirical cross-entropy between the label distribution and the model, and training drives the model toward the data distribution in the KL sense.

example.title: Cross-entropy for a classifier
example.problem: A classifier assigns probabilities (0.7, 0.2, 0.1) to three classes, and the true label is class 1 (a one-hot distribution). Compute the cross-entropy in nats.
example.solution: H(p, q) = −1 × ln 0.7 − 0 − 0 = 0.357 nats. For a one-hot target the entropy of p is 0, so the cross-entropy equals the KL divergence, 0.357. Probability 0.1 on the correct class would cost 2.30 nats.

list: **Perplexity** of a language model is 2^{cross-entropy in bits} (or e^{nats}): the effective number of equally likely choices per token. A model with 3 bits per token has perplexity 8. The cross-entropy is also the number of bits per token needed to compress text with the model (arithmetic coding), so prediction and compression are the same problem.
**Variational inference and VAEs** minimize KL(q ‖ posterior) and include the term KL(q(z | x) ‖ p(z)).
**Reinforcement learning** (TRPO, PPO, RLHF) limits the KL divergence between the new and old policy.
**Knowledge distillation** trains a small model to match the output distribution of a large one by minimizing KL.

**Maximum entropy principle**: among all distributions satisfying given constraints, choose the one with the greatest entropy, the least committal. It yields the uniform, exponential family and softmax forms (see Constrained Optimization).

body: The **differential entropy** of a density is h(X) = −∫f(x) ln f(x) dx. It can be negative (a uniform density on [0, a] has h = ln a, negative for a < 1). Among all densities with variance σ², the Gaussian has the maximum entropy, ½ ln(2πeσ²). The KL divergence between two univariate Gaussians has a closed form:

body.eq: KL( N(μ₁, σ₁²) ‖ N(μ₂, σ₂²) ) = ln(σ₂/σ₁) + ( σ₁² + (μ₁ − μ₂)² ) / (2σ₂²) − ½

example.title: KL between Gaussians
example.solution: With μ₁ = 0, σ₁ = 1, μ₂ = 1, σ₂ = 2: ln 2 + (1 + 1)/(2 · 4) − ½ = 0.693 + 0.25 − 0.5 = 0.443 nats. With μ₂ = 0, σ₂ = 1 it is 0 + 0.5 − 0.5 = 0, as required. The VAE's KL term for N(μ, σ²) against N(0, 1) is ½(μ² + σ² − ln σ² − 1), the same formula with the second distribution standard normal.

quiz.q: A source emits three symbols with probabilities 1/2, 1/4 and 1/4. What is its entropy?
quiz.why: H = ½(1) + ¼(2) + ¼(2) = 1.5 bits. The value log₂ 3 would be the entropy if the three symbols were equally likely, and it is the maximum for three outcomes.

quiz.q: A coin lands heads with probability 0.25. What is its entropy?
quiz.why: H = −0.25 log₂ 0.25 − 0.75 log₂ 0.75 = 0.5 + 0.311 = 0.811 bits. It is below the 1 bit of a fair coin, because the outcome is more predictable.

quiz.q: What is the entropy of a fair coin measured in nats?
quiz.why: With natural logarithms H = ln 2 = 0.693. The value 1.443 is the number of bits in one nat, which converts in the wrong direction.

quiz.q: In an ideal code, how long should the codeword be for a symbol of probability 1/16?
quiz.why: Codeword length should be about −log₂ p = log₂ 16 = 4 bits: rare symbols get long codes and frequent ones short codes.

quiz.q: A source has entropy 2.3 bits. Which average length is impossible for any prefix code for it?
quiz.why: Shannon's source coding theorem gives H ≤ L < H + 1, that is 2.3 ≤ L < 3.3. No code can average below the entropy.

quiz.q: H(X) = 2 bits and H(Y | X) = 0.5 bits. What is H(X, Y)?
quiz.why: The chain rule gives H(X, Y) = H(X) + H(Y | X) = 2.5. Subtracting would wrongly treat the conditional entropy as a saving rather than extra uncertainty.

quiz.q: Which inequality holds for every pair of discrete random variables?
quiz.why: Conditioning never increases entropy, with equality iff X and Y are independent. H(Y | X) can exceed H(X), and H(X, Y) is at least H(X).

quiz.q: Which statement about mutual information I(X; Y) is correct?
quiz.a: It is zero only if X and Y are independent, so it detects nonlinear dependence
wrong: It can be negative when X and Y are negatively correlated
It is zero whenever X and Y are uncorrelated
It equals the squared correlation coefficient
quiz.why: I(X; Y) ≥ 0 and vanishes exactly under independence. Uncorrelated variables, such as X and X² for symmetric X, can still have positive mutual information.

quiz.q: X → Y → Z is a Markov chain with I(X; Y) = 0.8 bits, and Z is computed from Y. What is true of I(X; Z)?
wrong: It can exceed 0.8 bits if the computation is nonlinear
quiz.why: The data processing inequality says that processing Y cannot create information about X. Equality is possible but not guaranteed.

quiz.q: A node has label entropy 1 bit. A split sends 60% of the data to a child with entropy 0.5 bits and 40% to a child with entropy 0.9 bits. What is the information gain?
quiz.why: H(Y | split) = 0.6(0.5) + 0.4(0.9) = 0.66, and the gain is 1 − 0.66 = 0.34. The value 0.66 is the remaining uncertainty, not the gain.

quiz.q: p = (0.5, 0.5) and q = (0.25, 0.75). What is KL(p ‖ q) in bits?
quiz.why: KL(p ‖ q) = 0.5 log₂(2) + 0.5 log₂(2/3) = 0.5 − 0.292 = 0.208. The value 0.19 is KL(q ‖ p), and 1.21 is the cross-entropy H(p, q).

quiz.q: The true label is a one-hot distribution, and the model gives the correct class probability 0.25. What is the cross-entropy in bits?
quiz.why: H(p, q) = −log₂ 0.25 = 2 bits. A one-hot target has zero entropy, so this equals KL(p ‖ q).

quiz.q: Which statement about KL divergence is false?
quiz.a: KL(p ‖ q) always equals KL(q ‖ p)
wrong: KL(p ‖ q) ≥ 0, with equality only when p = q
KL(p ‖ q) is infinite if q(x) = 0 where p(x) > 0
quiz.why: KL is asymmetric, so the two directions generally differ. The other three statements are Gibbs' inequality, the support condition and the cross-entropy identity.

quiz.q: p = (0.5, 0.5) and q = (1, 0). What are KL(p ‖ q) and KL(q ‖ p)?
quiz.why: KL(p ‖ q) is infinite because q assigns probability 0 to an outcome that p can produce. KL(q ‖ p) = 1 · log₂(1/0.5) = 1 bit, since q never produces the outcome where it is 0.

quiz.q: A single Gaussian is fitted to a two-peaked p by minimizing the reverse KL(q ‖ p), as in variational inference. What is typical of the result?
quiz.a: A narrow Gaussian on one peak
wrong: A broad Gaussian covering both peaks
A Gaussian centered between the peaks with a large variance
The same fit as maximum likelihood
quiz.why: Reverse KL punishes q for putting mass where p has little, so q is mode-seeking. Forward KL, which gives maximum likelihood, is mass-covering.

quiz.q: A language model has cross-entropy 2 nats per token. What is its perplexity?
quiz.why: Perplexity is the exponential of the cross-entropy in the same unit as the logarithm: e^{nats} (or 2^{bits}). Using base 2 on a value in nats gives the wrong 4.

quiz.q: In a VAE, the KL term for N(μ, σ²) against N(0, 1) is ½(μ² + σ² − ln σ² − 1). What is it for μ = 2 and σ = 1?
quiz.why: ½(4 + 1 − 0 − 1) = 2. With μ = 0 and σ = 1 the same formula gives 0, as it must for identical distributions.

quiz.q: What is the differential entropy of a uniform density on [0, 0.5], in nats?
quiz.why: For a uniform density on [0, a], h = ln a, which is negative for a < 1. Unlike discrete entropy, differential entropy can be negative.

summary: Entropy H(X) = −Σp log p is the expected surprise and the minimum average code length (H ≤ L < H + 1). It is maximal for the uniform distribution (log n) and zero for a certain outcome.

H(X, Y) = H(X) + H(Y | X). The mutual information I(X; Y) = H(Y) − H(Y | X) ≥ 0 measures any kind of dependence, and equals the information gain of a decision tree split. The data processing inequality says processing cannot add information.
Cross-entropy H(p, q) = H(p) + KL(p ‖ q). KL(p ‖ q) ≥ 0 (Gibbs), is zero iff p = q, and is asymmetric. Forward KL is mass-covering; reverse KL is mode-seeking.
Maximum likelihood minimizes KL(p_data ‖ p_θ); the classification loss is a cross-entropy; perplexity is 2^{bits per token}.
Gaussians: h = ½ ln(2πeσ²), the maximum entropy density for a given variance, and a closed-form KL that appears in VAEs.

problems.q: Compute the entropy in bits of the distribution (0.5, 0.25, 0.125, 0.0625, 0.0625).
p = (0.8, 0.2) and q = (0.5, 0.5). Compute KL(p ‖ q) and KL(q ‖ p) in bits.
X is a fair bit and Y = X (a perfect copy). Compute H(X), H(Y | X) and I(X; Y).
problems.solution: H(X) = 1 bit. Given X, Y is known, so H(Y | X) = 0. I(X; Y) = H(Y) − H(Y | X) = 1 bit: Y carries all the information of X.

problems.q: A binary classifier gives probability 0.8 to the correct class on 90% of examples and 0.3 on the other 10%. Compute the average cross-entropy in nats.
Show that the KL divergence from N(μ, σ²) to N(0, 1) is ½(μ² + σ² − ln σ² − 1), and evaluate it for μ = 0.5, σ = 1.
problems.solution: Set μ₁ = μ, σ₁ = σ, μ₂ = 0, σ₂ = 1 in the formula: ln(1/σ) + (σ² + μ²)/2 − ½ = ½(−ln σ² + σ² + μ² − 1). For μ = 0.5 and σ = 1: ½(0 + 1 + 0.25 − 1) = 0.125 nats.
